**Amplicon length analysis.** Mutations that affect the length of a DNA amplicon (e.g., deletions or expansions) can be easily detected by PCR if different forms of the indel do not pose barriers to amplification. As discussed earlier, several diseases, such as FXS, are associated with alterations in **trinucleotide repeats**. Two primers that flank the region containing the trinucleotide repeats at the 59 end of the *FMR1* gene can be used to amplify the intervening sequences. Because there are differences in the number of repeats, the size of the PCR products obtained from normal allele(s), or those with a premutation, is quite different and can be distinguished by gel electrophoresis. An important caveat is that if the trinucleotide expansion is so large that it cannot be amplified by conventional PCR, Southern blot analysis of genomic DNA may have to be performed. As discussed earlier, large expansions are not uncommon in FXS.

**Real-time PCR.** A variety of PCR-based technologies that use fluorophore indicators can detect and quantify the presence of particular nucleic acid sequences in real time (i.e., assessing the PCR product during the exponential phase of DNA amplification rather than post- PCR). These quantitative PCR (qPCR) reactions are most often used to monitor the burden of disease in cancers bearing characteristic genetic lesions in the blood or in tissues (e.g., the level of BCR-ABL fusion mRNA transcripts in patients with **CML**), or the infectious load of certain viruses (e.g., HIV, Epstein-Barr virus). The measured target can be genomic DNA or RNA that has been reverse transcribed to cDNA before the qPCR (reverse transcription PCR or RT-PCR).
Large-Scale Genomic Alterations

A significant number of genetic lesions involve large deletions, duplications, or more complex rearrangements with variable breakpoints, and are not readily amenable to detection using PCR. Long read sequencing technologies and high molecular weight DNA strand imaging methods are poised for clinical translation in this space. In the meantime, they are commonly studied using a variety of hybridization-based techniques.

Array Technology

FISH requires prior knowledge of the one or few specific chromosomal regions suspected of being altered in the test sample. However, genomic abnormalities can also be detected without prior knowledge by performing genome-wide surveys using microarray technology, whole-genome sequencing, or molecular imaging platforms. The first of these is considered further here. First-generation microarray platforms were designed for comparative genomic hybridization (CGH), while newer platforms incorporate single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) genotyping approaches, offering multiple benefits.

**Array-based comparative genomic hybridization (CGH).** In array CGH, equal amounts of test DNA and a reference (normal) DNA are labeled with two different fluorescent dyes (e.g., Cy3). The samples are then mixed and hybridized to an array spotted with DNA probes that span unique sequences in the human genome at regularly spaced intervals. At each chromosomal probe location, binding of the labeled DNA from the two samples is compared. If the two samples are equal (i.e., the test sample is diploid), all spots on the array will fluoresce yellow due to equal admixture of green and red dyes. In contrast, if the test sample has a deletion or duplication, the probe spots corresponding to it will show skewing toward red or green (depending on gain or loss of material), allowing highly accurate determination of even focal copy number gain or loss anywhere across the genome. The smallest gains and losses that can be detected depend on the density of the tiling probes (i.e., arrays with a probe placed every 200 base pairs will have greater resolution for small gains and losses as compared with arrays with a probe placed every kilobase), and usually several probes corresponding to contiguous genomic sequences need to be involved for the interval gain or loss to be detected.

**Single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping arrays.** Newer genomic tiling arrays are based on a similar concept, but some or all of the probes are designed to identify SNP sites genome-wide (i.e., a DNA sample binds in a genotype-dependent manner), which provides a number of advantages. As discussed in Chapter 1, SNPs are the most common type of DNA polymorphism, occurring on average approximately every 1000 nucleotides throughout the genome. They serve both as a physical landmark within the genome and as a genetic marker whose transmission can be followed from parent to child.

There are several testing platforms using different methodologies that allow SNPs to be analyzed genome-wide on arrays; details of these methods are beyond the scope of this discussion. Like CGH probes, these methods involving SNPs can be used to make copy number variation (CNV) calls, but by discriminating between SNP alleles at each particular location they also provide genotype (haplotype) information (Fig. 5.34).

Polymorphic Markers

Clinical detection of disease-specific mutations is possible only if the gene responsible for the disorder is known and its sequence has been identified. If the exact nature of the genetic aberration is not known, or if testing for the primary defect is technically challenging or unfeasible, diagnostic laboratories can take advantage of the phenomenon of linkage. In humans, two DNA loci neighboring one another on the same chromosome are almost certain to cosegregate during meiosis due to the extremely low chance of a crossover event happening between them. Generally, the closer two loci are, the higher the probability that they will travel together in family pedigrees; in some regions of the genome, linkage disequilibrium between two markers segregating in a population can extend over long distances. In the event of a challenging or unknown pathogenic allele, a diagnostic laboratory can sometimes choose surrogate markers that travel together on the same strand and “tag” the mutated sequence and use their presence to infer inheritance of the mutated or normal allele in the context of the family pedigree.

The two types of genetic polymorphisms most useful for linkage analysis are SNPs (described earlier) and repeat-length polymorphisms known as minisatellite and microsatellite repeats. Human DNA contains short repetitive sequences of DNA giving rise to what are called repeat-length polymorphisms. These polymorphisms are often subdivided based on their length into microsatellite repeats and minisatellite repeats. Microsatellites are usually less than 1 kb and are characterized by a repeat size of 1 to 6 bp. Minisatellite repeats, by comparison, are larger (1 to 3 kb), and the repeat motif is usually 10 to 100 bp. The number of repeats, both in microsatellites and in minisatellites, can be extremely variable within a given population, and hence these stretches of DNA can be used to establish genetic identity. Most commonly, minisatellites known as variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs) are genotyped for this purpose, which involves PCR amplification using primers that flank the repeat region. Fig. 5.35 depicts the application of microsatellite linkage analysis to the PKD1 gene (historically very difficult to sequence) for the familial diagnosis of adult **polycystic kidney disease**. In this example, the longest VNTR sequence is linked in the family to the disease allele and can be used to track its transmission.

Assays to detect genetic polymorphisms are also important in many other areas of medicine, including in the determination of relatedness and identity in transplantation, paternity testing, and forensic medicine. Since VNTR markers occur throughout the human genome and have such a high level of polymorphism, they are ideal for differentiating between two individuals and to follow transmission of the marker from parent to child. Assays employing PCR amplification of informative markers are now routinely used for determining paternity and for criminal investigations. PCR can be performed even with highly degraded biologic samples, allowing DNA testing to play a central role in forensic identifications. The same assays are used in patients following allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant to detect and quantify bone marrow chimerism, which is evaluated by assessing the relative amounts of donor-derived and recipient-derived DNA.
Epigenetic Alterations

Epigenetics is defined as the study of chemical modification of DNA or chromatin that do not alter the DNA sequence itself. As described earlier, examples of such modifications include CpG dinucleotide methylation of DNA and methylation and acetylation of histone proteins (Chapter 1). Diagnosis of an increasing number of diseases involves the analysis of promoter methylation—for example, FXS, in which hypermethylation results in *FMR1* silencing. Methylation analysis is also essential in the diagnosis of **Prader-Willi syndrome** and **Angelman syndrome**.

Special techniques are needed to detect DNA methylation. One approach is to treat genomic DNA with sodium bisulfite, a chemical that converts unmethylated cytosine (C) to uracil (U), which acts like thy-mine (T) in downstream reactions. Methylated cytosines are protected from modification and remain unchanged (C). After treatment, it is then straightforward to discriminate the unmethylated (modified)
DNA from the methylated (unmodified) DNA by DNA sequencing.

Alternative approaches for assaying DNA methylation include those that depend on proteins which selectively bind to methylated DNA (e.g., enriching for DNA using methyl-CpG binding proteins) or alter the DNA (e.g., using methylation sensitive restriction enzymes).

Still other methods recognize modified DNA bases directly, for example, based on changes in the kinetics of DNA polymerase copying a template or methylation-specific changes in the ionic patterns produced as DNA strands are pulled through nanopore sequencers.

Next-Generation Sequencing

Next-generation sequencing is a term used to describe several newer DNA sequencing technologies that produce very large amounts of sequence data in a massively parallel manner. These technologies have revolutionized biomedical research and molecular diagnostics.

The factors propelling rapid adoption of NGS are price and throughput: NGS allows us to perform otherwise impossibly comprehensive (e.g., covering all exons) or “deep” (high coverage) analyses at extremely low cost.

One feature that makes NGS far more clinically applicable than Sanger sequencing is its input sample requirement. Whereas Sanger sequencing requires a single homogeneous template DNA (usually a specific PCR product), NGS has no such requirement: any DNA from almost any source can be used. Because Sanger sequencing essentially provides an “average” result for a particular DNA region in a sample, samples with substantial sequence heterogeneity among input DNA molecules produce uninterpretable results. NGS, by contrast, is well suited to analysis of heterogeneous DNA samples due to the application of three common basic principles (Fig. 5.36).
**Spatial separation.** At the beginning of the procedure, individual DNA molecules are physically isolated from each other in space.
The specifics of this process are platform dependent.

**Local amplification.** After separation, the individual DNA molecules are amplified in place using a limited number of PCR cycles. Amplification is necessary so that sufficient signal can be generated to ensure detection and accuracy.

**Parallel sequencing.** The amplified DNA molecules are then simultaneously sequenced by the addition of polymerases and other re-agents, with each spatially separated and amplified original molecule yielding a “read” corresponding to its sequence. Sequence reads from NGS instruments are generally short, less than 500 bp.
Bioinformatics

Each NGS analysis generates a staggering amount of sequence data; for high throughput sequencing instruments, this amounts to billions of DNA reads and terabytes (Tb) of data per day, enough to produce a high-quality sequence spanning an entire human genome. The downstream analysis is sufficiently complex that specialized training in bioinformatics is needed. Computational “pipelines” vary widely across applications and sample types, and a detailed discussion is beyond the scope of this text. However, it is worth describing the basic steps necessary to process this type of data.
**Alignment.** Alignment is the process by which the sequencing reads from a sample are mapped to a reference genome, allowing them to be viewed and interpreted in context.
**Variant calling.** This process involves a systematic comparison of the sequence data from a sample with the reference sequence.

Samples are typically sequenced to sufficient coverage that germline polymorphisms in the target intervals are identified. The more reads that cover a particular location (sequencing depth), the more likely that variants with low variant allele frequency (VAF) in a sample will be detected.

**Variant annotation and interpretation.** Variants can be annotated with various pieces of information (e.g., gene name, coding change and protein effect predictions, information from databases listing commonly occurring as well as pathogenic variants, clinical information). Once reviewed by the clinical laboratory, the annotated data are ready for reporting. Because the pace of advances in genetics and genomics has far outpaced the knowledge of the typical clinician, an important part of this report is a brief description of the biological and clinical significance of each pathogenic variant, which can be numerous in the case of some cancers.

**Mutational signature calling.** In addition to totaling up individual mutations, informatics algorithms have been developed that detect patterns of mutations that point to particular environmental exposures (e.g., ultraviolet light, smoking) or underlying defects in DNA repair. These have become clinically relevant with the discovery that cancers with high tumor mutational burden (TMB) or acquired defects in mismatch repair genes that lead to microsatellite instability (MSI) tend to be responsive to immune checkpoint inhibitors (Chapter 7). Based on this observation, many clinical laboratories are now “calling” the TMB and MSI status of cancers based on NGS results.
Clinical Applications of Next-Generation DNA Sequencing

As discussed, any DNA sample can be analyzed by NGS. However, the DNA needs to first be prepared for sequencing by constructing a library of short DNA sequences that are enriched for genomic regions of interest (e.g., particular exons or the “whole exome”). There are several methods for NGS library preparation from genomic DNA. In the clinical laboratories, most applications of NGS are targeted toward constitutional genetic disease and cancer diagnostics, using a few different basic approaches:

**Targeted sequencing.** Most current clinical laboratory NGS tests fall in this category. Targeted sequencing is focused on the exons of a carefully selected panel of genes, which maximizes sequencing depth while minimizing costs and the time and expense required for interpretation and clinical reporting. Sample preparation for targeted sequencing is typically performed by enriching sequences in an NGS library by hybrid capture using a panel of synthesized biotinylated probes complementary to the regions of interest. Single-gene NGS assays for inherited disorders are also becoming more common, and many laboratories that previously performed costly Sanger sequencing of multiple PCR products (i.e., to enable comprehensive *CFTR* sequencing) are now moving these assays to NGS platforms. Targeted NGS with gene panels is also now com-monplace in evaluating individuals with genetic diseases such as cardiomyopathy and congenital deafness. In cancer testing, gene panels are widely used to perform detailed tumor profiling. Each tumor has a unique set of somatic mutations, and these assays aim to detect as many treatable or prognostic mutations as possible to offer individually tailored patient care. Increasingly, repeat testing at the time of disease recurrence is also being performed to understand mechanisms of drug resistance, which can serve to guide the selection of second-line therapies.

**Whole-exome sequencing (WES).** WES is a more expansive type of targeted sequencing, in which hundreds of thousands of probes are used to enrich for the roughly 1.5% of the genome that consists of protein-encoding exons prior to NGS. It has led to some success stories in identifying the molecular basis for constitutional genetic diseases, allowing physicians to deliver answers and even therapies for children with orphan diseases who had suffered through prolonged and unsuccessful diagnostic odysseys. WES is also used in oncology, mostly in the research setting to discover alterations in infrequently mutated genes.

**Whole-genome sequencing (WGS).** WGS is the most comprehensive type of DNA analysis that can be performed on an individual. Current indications for use in medical genetics are mostly limited to cases where exome sequencing has failed to provide an answer, but the clinical suspicion of genetic disease remains high. For cancer applications, WGS of sufficient depth can detect noncoding mutations and novel structural rearrangements (e.g., insertions, deletions, translocations) that may be clinically relevant, but relatively high costs, slow turnaround times, and significant informatics challenges still preclude its routine use in clinical practice.
Liquid Biopsies and ctDNA Analysis

Because NGS can provide information from few starting molecules and can detect infrequent alleles in admixtures of normal and abnormal DNA, it is opening a field of cancer biomarker detection in the peripheral blood. In some clinical scenarios, relatively noninvasive blood draws (being termed “liquid biopsies”) can recover sufficient material shed from tumor cells and provide information that previously required direct surgical sampling (Fig. 5.37). Genomic DNA from tumors can exist in the blood both in circulating tumor cells that detach from solid tumor site(s) or “free” in the circulation, released by dead or dying cells.

Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) is recognizable as abnormal either because of the presence of recurrent cancer-driving point mutations, the presence of “passenger mutations” inherent to an individual’s tumor (creating a “bespoke” mutation signature unique to that patient), or the existence of epigenetic alterations associated with malignancy. Because DNA methylation patterns are highly dependent on cell types, epigenetic signatures can be used not only to indicate the presence of a cancer, but also can inform its origin. Other highly sensitive assays are being applied to detect trace proteins and tumor cell extracellular vesicles (exosomes) which may compliment ctDNA analyses.

This is a very active area of investigation and innovation in cancer diagnostics, where there are significant needs for biomarkers: (1) to improve detection of early stage, and thus more treatable malignancies; (2) to reduce false positives, false negatives, and the expense of would-be screening tests; (3) to predict and monitor therapeutic responses; and (4) to indicate persistence of minimal residual disease to inform therapeutic decision-making.
